But New York, machine learning and not good only mean something together. An n-gram is n words in a row. Two make a bigram, three make a trigram. Slide a window two words wide along the quick brown fox jumps, one step at a time, so the windows overlap. Five words give four bigrams, and three trigrams: the number of words, minus n, plus one.

Why bother? Compare the food was good with the food was not good. As sets of single words, they differ by one word: not. As bigrams, only one of them has not good, and that's a feature a sentiment model can learn is negative. Counting bigrams finds phrases, too. In three short lines about machine learning, the top pair is machine learning, three times. Over all of Emma, keep the pairs with no stopword in them, and out walks the cast: Mister Knightley, Missus Weston, Mister Elton. [curious] So if two words in a row help, would five help more?

Usually not. Count Emma's n-grams, and see how many turn up only once. For single words, thirty-nine percent. For bigrams, seventy-three. Trigrams, ninety. By five in a row, ninety-nine. A count of one tells you almost nothing. That's sparsity, and it gets worse with every word you add to the window. So bigrams and trigrams are the sweet spot: enough order to help, and common enough to count. But a model wants numbers, not lists of words. So next, we'll turn text into features.
